title: The 15 essential Claude Code terms
source: Lines are exactly as written in the lyrics. Times come from a word-level transcription of the finished track, aligned to the written words; a word the transcription heard differently takes a time between its neighbours.

lines.text: What's up y'all. I know you just learned a whole lot at the dojo,
and it's hard to keep all of it in your head.
So here's a little rap to lock in the fifteen essential terms.
Make sure you stretch those typing fingers before you start.

sections.definition: The window where you type commands, also called the CLI, the command-line interface. It is where Claude Code started, and it also runs in VS Code, JetBrains, the desktop app, and the web.

lines.text: Number one, the Terminal, that black window on the screen,
you type in your commands and tell it just what you mean.
The fancy name for typing there is called the C L I,
command-line interface, where Claude lives, now you know why.

sections.definition: More than a chatbot. You give it a goal, and it opens your files and does the work to see it through.

lines.text: Number two, the Agent, it does way more than chat,
it opens up your files and it handles all of that.
You give it a goal and it sees the mission through,
a chatbot only talks, but an agent works for you.

sections.definition: A little bit of text. Your words get chopped into tokens, and every token is billed, so tight prompts cost less.

lines.text: Number three, the Token, every word gets chopped in two,
little bits of text, and every bit is billed to you.
The more of them you spend, the more the meter's gonna climb,
so keep your prompting tight and save your money and your time.

sections.definition: Claude’s working memory for a session: the conversation, the files it read, and your standing instructions. When it fills up, Claude Code summarizes the early part, so details can drop out. Run /compact yourself, or start fresh with /clear when you switch tasks.

lines.text: Number four, Context Window, that's where memory lives,
it holds on to everything the conversation gives.
But when the window fills right up, the early stuff, it fades,
so start a brand new session when you've worked it hard for days.

sections.definition: A file of your rules that Claude reads every session, so you write them down once.

lines.text: Number five, CLAUDE dot M D, that's the memory card,
a file with your rules so remembering's not hard.
It reads it every session, so it knows just where you stand,
write it down one time and every session goes as planned.

sections.definition: Claude writes out every step first and changes nothing until you give it the green light.

lines.text: Number six is Plan Mode, look before you leap,
it writes out every step in a list for you to keep.
Nothing gets changed until you give it the green light,
measure twice and cut once, and the code comes out right.

sections.definition: Save points, one for each prompt you send. Press Esc twice or run /rewind to roll Claude’s file edits back to one. They do not undo what a shell command changed, so keep using git.

lines.text: Number seven, Checkpoints, that's a save point in time,
if a big change breaks things you can rewind on a dime.
No need to panic when the edit goes wrong,
roll back to the checkpoint and keep moving along.

sections.definition: How deeply Claude thinks. Turn it up for hard problems, knowing that deeper takes longer and costs more.

lines.text: Number eight, Effort Level, how deep should it think?
Crank it up for hard stuff, it'll reason on the brink.
But deeper takes longer and it costs a little more,
so match it to the task, that's what the dial is for.
Whew. That's eight already.
Are y'all ready for more?
... Are you sure?
... Alright, seems like y'all are ready. Let's go.

sections.definition: A workflow on repeat: a recipe Claude follows for one kind of job, such as security or design.

lines.text: Number nine is Skills, that's a workflow on repeat,
a recipe it follows so the finish stays neat.
There's one for security, and design, and browsing too,
load the right one up and it knows just what to do.

sections.definition: A bundle you install in one step from a marketplace. It can hold skills, hooks, subagents, and MCP servers.

lines.text: Number ten, the Plugin, it's a bundle you install,
a box of ready skills, and one download grabs them all.

sections.definition: The Model Context Protocol: one standard way to plug tools and systems into Claude.

lines.text: Eleven, MCP, Model Context Protocol,
one standard way to plug in tools, a plug that fits them all.
Databases, servers, and the systems that you run,
speak a common language and connect them one by one.

sections.definition: MCP in action: a hookup to an app like Gmail, Calendar, Slack, or Drive, so Claude can reach it.

lines.text: Twelve is the Connector, MCP in action live,
it hooks up Gmail, Calendar, your Slack, and your Drive.
Once you've got it plugged in, Claude can reach them all the same,
ask it for your schedule and it calls them out by name.

sections.definition: An automatic move. You set it up once, and a trigger fires it without you asking.

lines.text: Thirteen is the Hook, that's an automatic move,
a trigger fires it off and the hook slides in the groove.
You set it up one time and you never have to ask,
it fires on its own, right behind the task.

sections.definition: Helpers the main agent hands work to, such as one running the tests while another reads the code.

lines.text: Fourteen, Subagents, that's the helpers on the team,
the main one delegates like a coach who's got a scheme.
One runs all the tests while another reads the code,
splitting up the work will always lighten up the load.

sections.definition: The places you use Claude. In the Claude app those are Chat, Cowork, and Code. Claude Code itself runs on several surfaces: the terminal, VS Code, JetBrains, the desktop app, and the web.

lines.text: Last one, Work Surfaces, three doors to the same brain,
Chat for quick conversation, keeping questions plain.
Cowork handles desk work, the projects and the grind,
and Code is for the software, three doors, one mind.
Congratulations, you made it through all fifteen.
You're basically fluent in Claude Code now.
Let's try one, just to check.
A standard way to plug your tools into Claude...
That's right. MCP.
Now you try the rest.
That's all I've got y'all. These fifteen terms will take you far,
and I'm so proud of how far you've already come.
Peace, have a blessed day, and I'll see you at the dojo.
